```{r setup, include = FALSE}
have_python <- threadfin::threadfin_available()
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = have_python,
  fig.width = 9, fig.height = 6.5, dpi = 72, fig.retina = 1, out.width = "100%"
)
```

This vignette runs Threadfin from R on a repertoire simulated by the Python package, so it needs no download and
the right answer is known. Every number and figure comes from the Python package itself: the R functions convert
the inputs, call Threadfin and hand back data frames.
`r if (!have_python) "*The Python package threadfin was not available when this vignette was built, so the code below is shown without its output.*"`

## Set up once

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("Reynold4k/threadfinR")
threadfin::install_threadfin()     # Python environment "r-threadfin": threadfin and Dandelion from PyPI
```

Restart R afterwards; `library(threadfin)` then finds the environment on its own.

```{r library}
library(threadfin)
```

## A repertoire with a known answer

`simulate_repertoire()` makes paired data the way Threadfin sees them: cells in clones, clones in four donors,
each donor sampled in three libraries (`context`), and every clone drawn from one of four programmes
(`true_programme`) that set how its cells are spread over six cell states (`true_state`). The simulation already
has clone ids and an expression embedding, so no receptor table is needed here.

```{r simulate}
adata <- simulate_repertoire(n_clones = 600, random_state = 0)
adata
```

## One call

```{r run}
res <- run_threadfin(
  adata,
  donor_key = "donor",          # clones are compared within individuals
  sample_key = "context",       # each clone is compared with the cells sampled alongside it
  basis = "X_pca",              # an existing embedding; without it Threadfin builds one from raw counts
  state_key = "true_state",     # describes the programmes by cell state
  test = "true_programme",      # a label to test against the clones
  verbose = FALSE
)
res
```

`summary(res)` prints Threadfin's plain-language report:

```{r summary}
summary(res)
```

Every part of it is a data frame. Are cells of one clone more alike than cells of different clones? Clone identity
explains `icc` of the variance of cell states, against `null_mean` when clone labels are shuffled within each
library:

```{r coherence}
res$coherence[, c("icc", "null_mean", "excess", "p_value", "strata_key")]
```

One row per clone with two or more cells, with its reliability, its place on the clone map and its programme:

```{r clones}
head(res$clones[, c("clone_id", "n_cells", "reliability", "x", "y", "clone_programme", "confidence")])
res$programmes
```

How much of the difference between clones does a label explain, against the same label shuffled among clones of
the same donor and size?

```{r tests}
res$profile_tests[, c("label", "r2", "null_mean", "excess_r2", "p_value", "n_clones")]
```

Because the data are simulated, the programmes Threadfin found can be checked against the simulated ones:

```{r check}
simulated <- clone_labels(adata, "true_programme")      # one value per clone
table(simulated = simulated[res$clones$clone_id], found = res$clones$clone_programme)
```

`res$cells` has the clone and programme of every cell, to add to a Seurat object or a SingleCellExperiment, and
`res$methods` is a Methods paragraph with the settings and package versions used.

## Figures

The overview: the clone map with one panel per programme, the coherence test, programme stability and the
composition of each programme in cell states.

```{r overview}
plot_overview(res)
```

`plot_overview(res, file = "threadfin_overview.pdf")` writes Threadfin's own PDF. The clone map can be coloured by
any column of the clone table:

```{r map, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 5}
plot_clone_map(res, color = "n_cells")
```

`plot_threadfin()` draws every other figure of `threadfin.pl` (`"coherence"`, `"stability"`, `"association"`,
`"memory"`, `"label_effects"`, `"heritability"`, ...).

## Your own data

```{r own-data, eval = FALSE}
# files: raw counts with the donor and sample of each cell, and Cell Ranger's contigs
res <- run_threadfin("b_cells.h5ad", bcr = "filtered_contig_annotations.csv",
                     donor_key = "donor", sample_key = "sample", n_jobs = 8)

# a Seurat object (raw counts in the "counts" layer) with the contigs as a data frame
contigs <- read.csv("filtered_contig_annotations.csv")
res <- run_threadfin(seurat_obj, bcr = contigs, donor_key = "donor", sample_key = "sample",
                     test = c("isotype", "antigen_binding"))

# a SingleCellExperiment, several tissues per donor: describe clones relative to the donor and shuffle
# clone labels within libraries
res <- run_threadfin(sce, bcr = "airr_rearrangement.tsv", donor_key = "donor", sample_key = "donor",
                     strata_key = "library", test = "tissue")

# T cells: the TCR contigs as bcr; clones called elsewhere: a clone_id column and no bcr
res <- run_threadfin(seurat_obj, donor_key = "donor", sample_key = "sample")

# back to the Seurat object
seurat_obj$clone_programme <- res$cells$clone_programme[match(colnames(seurat_obj), res$cells$cell)]
```

Clones are called with Dandelion's paired heavy- and light-chain definition within each donor, under Python's
string-hash seed 0, so the clone ids are the same in every session (see `?define_clones_dandelion`). The cell names
of the contig table must match those of the expression data; with several libraries, give both the same prefixes
(Threadfin's Tutorial 2, section 4).

## Step by step

The analysis steps of Threadfin's Tutorial 4 are R functions too. They work on an AnnData and write their results
into it, as in Python, so later steps find them; `as_anndata()` makes one from a file, a Seurat object or a
SingleCellExperiment. Here a simulated time course: four donors, each sampled at two time points, in which clones
keep their programme with probability 0.8.

```{r steps}
tc <- simulate_repertoire(n_clones = 400, n_timepoints = 2, memory = 0.8, random_state = 0)
profiles <- clone_profiles(tc, basis = "X_pca", context_key = "context", donor_key = "donor",
                           representation = "kernel", verbose = FALSE)
nrow(profiles)
coh <- clonal_coherence(tc, strata_key = "context", verbose = FALSE)
as.data.frame(coh)[, c("icc", "null_mean", "p_value")]
map <- embed_clones(tc, verbose = FALSE)
programmes <- find_programmes(tc, verbose = FALSE)
programmes[, c("programme", "n_clones", "stability")]
```

Do clones keep their state between the time points?

```{r memory}
mem <- clonal_memory(tc, "timepoint", verbose = FALSE)
c(index = mem$memory_index, lower = mem$memory_index_ci[1], upper = mem$memory_index_ci[2], p = mem$p_value)
```

```{r memory-figure, fig.width = 3.5, fig.height = 3.5, out.width = "40%"}
plot_memory(mem)
```

Further steps: `profile_association()` and `association_test()` test labels, `export_lag()` measures how much less
mutated a clone's ASCs (antibody-secreting cells) are than its own germinal-centre cells,
`gene_heritability()`, `programme_markers()` and `landscape_genes()` name the genes behind the clone landscape.

## Saving

```{r save}
files <- save_threadfin(res, tempdir())
basename(files)
again <- read_threadfin(files[["h5ad"]])
identical(again$summary, res$summary)
```

## Everything else

`tf` is the Python package itself, with the names of the
[Python function reference](https://github.com/Reynold4k/Threadfin/blob/main/docs/API.md):

```{r tf}
tf$`__version__`
head(names(tf$tl), 12)
```

For example `tf$tl$tune_clone_map()` or `tf$tl$lineage_heritability()`; results of this package pass to them
as their Python objects (`py_object(res)$adata`). Threadfin's
[tutorials](https://github.com/Reynold4k/Threadfin/tree/main/docs/tutorials) explain each analysis in depth.
